title: Do Androids Dream of Electric Seating Plans?
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Kenyon writes a speculative-fiction piece imagining English education from 2027 to the 2030s, tracing how a government-and-Google project to train AI on 'good classroom instruction' -- using a real teacher's recorded likeness -- metastasizes into a nationwide system of AI deepfake teachers delivering entire subjects to classes of 250+ students, with human staff reduced to minimum-wage 'Behaviour Monitors.' The piece follows the economic logic step by step: AI supply-teacher packages undercut agency rates, disadvantaged schools with high staff turnover adopt them first, staffing costs fall from 70-85% of school budgets to just above 30%, and a new national curriculum is eventually redesigned specifically to be deliverable by AI rather than human teachers, over union objections that go nowhere as new teachers who never knew anything else stop objecting. Kenyon uses invented headlines (BBC News, Computer Weekly, Microsoft product announcements) to make the trajectory feel like an extrapolation of real, currently visible pressures -- class-size growth, recruitment shortages, ed-tech marketing to underfunded schools -- rather than pure fantasy. The piece ends ambiguously on outcomes: some scores rise (via redefined, 'easier' reading-age benchmarks) while national test rankings stagnate, and the story closes on competing narratives about whether the erosion of small classes and human relationship-building was worth the cost savings, or whether that complaint is just outdated nostalgia.
points: Kenyon's speculative arc traces a specific mechanism of professional displacement: teachers are initially paid to have their own teaching likeness recorded for 'AI training,' not realizing this recording later becomes the product that eventually replaces classroom teachers of that subject entirely.

The piece is explicit about the economic driver, not just the technology: AI-teacher packages are adopted first by disadvantaged, high-turnover schools because they are cheaper than supply agencies, and national adoption follows because staffing costs are the largest line item in a school budget (70-85%, falling to ~30%).

He depicts the curriculum itself being redesigned by tech companies specifically to be deliverable by AI rather than by teachers, reframing curriculum design as a lever of workforce replacement rather than a purely pedagogical decision.

The story's ending deliberately avoids a clean verdict on outcomes -- test scores are mixed and redefined rather than clearly better or worse -- which frames the piece as a critique of how quietly and ambiguously such a transition could be normalized rather than a simple doomsday warning.
quotes: This was a UK Government project, funded by Google, to train their AI on what good classroom instruction looks like. James was paid for this and Elysium Learning Trust was keen to take part as they are a 'Forward Thinking' organisation, always striving to keep up to date with the latest research and EduTech.

ClassAI is a suite, offered by Google, that not only provided a suite of AI deepfake teachers to deliver expert content, but also comes with 30 AI powered tablets that replaced the student’s antiquated mini-whiteboards.
With large boards in front of entire year groups of 250+, staffing has reduced to little more than 2 or 3 Behaviour Monitors ensuring pupils remain on task.

It wasn’t a curriculum designed to be delivered by their members, they said. It was designed to be implemented by AI images of colleagues who, since their initial recordings back in 2027, have left the profession.

The DfEAII is happy. Every student has their own personalised tutor and access to expert teaching. The treasury is even happier. Back in 2026, 70-85% of a schools budget was staffing, now its a touch above 30%.

Some argue that we should return to the ‘old’ style of teaching, where one teacher teaches a small class of 35. It is argued that the relationship building and social elements that used to exist in schools has been eroded in favour of cost saving. Some say this is just typical of the Millennial mentality of a bygone era that never truly existed in the first place.
